comment: This principle states that countries should ground implementations in open standards that "reduce dependency on proprietary technology", and then names a single direction: "The architecture points to FHIR-based approaches as the direction of travel" (lines 233–234). No information-model formalism is named anywhere in the principle, and information models appear at line 235 only as something to be distributed, not as something to be expressed in a standard. This is inconsistent with the guidance's own treatment elsewhere: Annex D.1 lists EHRbase, "an open-source, openEHR-conformant clinical data repository that stores and queries health data against openEHR archetypes and templates", as an illustrative Lifelong Health Record implementation (page 230, lines 36–37); Appendix C page 175, functional requirement 2, status Required, obliges the LIMR to support openEHR archetypes and templates; and page 174 lines 81–85 make multi-formalism support a core attribute. A design principle that names one family as the direction of travel, while the component specifications require another alongside it, will be read by procurement teams as settling a question the rest of the document leaves open.

public.text: This principle states that countries should ground implementations in open standards that "reduce dependency on proprietary technology", and then names a single direction: "The architecture points to FHIR-based approaches as the direction of travel" (lines 233–234). No information-model formalism is named anywhere in the principle, and information models appear at line 235 only as something to be distributed, not as something to be expressed in a standard. This is inconsistent with the guidance's own treatment elsewhere: Annex D.1 lists EHRbase, "an open-source, openEHR-conformant clinical data repository that stores and queries health data against openEHR archetypes and templates", as an illustrative Lifelong Health Record implementation (page 230, lines 36–37); Appendix C page 175, functional requirement 2, status Required, obliges the LIMR to support openEHR archetypes and templates; and page 174 lines 81–85 make multi-formalism support a core attribute. A design principle that names one family as the direction of travel, while the component specifications require another alongside it, will be read by procurement teams as settling a question the rest of the document leaves open.
public.suggestedRevision: Amend lines 233–238 to express the direction of travel by layer rather than as a single family, for example: "The architecture points to open, openly governed standards as the direction of travel — HL7 FHIR for exchange services and transactions, an open information-model formalism such as openEHR archetypes and templates or ISO 13606 for the logical structure of persisted clinical data, and established classifications and terminologies for coded meaning — while accommodating countries at different stages of readiness …".
